newsitem.title: USA: Pre-refunding talk stirs in U.S. Treasury market.
newsitem.headline: Pre-refunding talk stirs in U.S. Treasury market.

text.p: Renewed talk that the U.S. Treasury may shrink the size of its upcoming refunding effort once again haunted Wall Street on Friday, sending money market players scrambling to sort through rumor, fact and innuendo.

Talk swept the bond market that the Treasury Advisory Committee, which channels the views of bond traders to the Treasury Department, had distributed a letter to primary dealerships. This letter was said to have requested dealers' opinions on a suggested make-up for the August refunding.
No confirmation that the document was sent was immediately available.
The rumored letter was said to have listed discussion topics for when the Committee meets with various dealers. Such meetings take place on a quarterly basis prior to each Treasury refunding.
Market sources said one of the topics mentioned in the alledged letter centered on recommendations regarding possible cutbacks in the size of next month's quarterly sale of government debt.
"It makes sense to me that the issue is part of this letter," one Wall Street banker said, adding that it was normal for the Committee to ask about auction-cycle recommendations.
In a meeting in January, for example, one of the issues discussed with dealers was the viability of the Treasury's inflation-protected securities (TIPS) program.
This time around, however, the discussion might become increasingly heated because a shrinking U.S. public deficit reduces the Treasury's borrowing needs.
"Everyone is expecting (cut backs)," said one trader at a U.S. primary dealership.
"But what the dealers recommend to the Advisory Committee, what the Advisory Committee suggests to the Treasury and what the Treasury actually decides are three different things."
Market sources said the debate among dealers now centers on either scrapping or scaling back the size of the 10- and 30-year tranches.
"One of the things that has been recommended to the Treasury is that they eliminate two of the 10-year auctions, or they eliminate the TIPS," one source said.
The Treasury's current auction cycle calls for quarterly sales of three-, 10-year notes and 30-year bonds.
Apart from the refunding problem, another source said that because of the TIPS sales, the Treasury may not necessarily need end-of-quarter five-year note auctions either.

"You have money maturing (at that time), but at the end of the quarter we normally run very high cash balances and they can in turn use the settlement from the TIPS to replace the fives," the source said.
(( -- Jose Paulo Vicente and Jacqueline Hurlock, 212-859-1660 ))
